summary: Administration reported on enrollment, transfers, class sizes, transportation, and pest concerns. Staff also presented an update on the behavioral health support system, MTSS-B. The committee approved the consent agenda and a personnel report.

BOARD OF SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
 
Monday, September 28, 2026 6:30 p.m.  
 
5:30 p.m. –  Non-Meeting with Legal Counsel – exempt from public disclosure under the 
provisions of RSA 91-A:2, I (b) consultation with legal counsel. 
 
 
1. Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. 
 
2. Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance. 
 
Mayor Ruais welcomed Principal Newman and students from Beech Street Elementary School to 
lead the Pledge of Allegiance. Committee Members Taylor and Potter introduced the students: 
 
Beech Street Elementary School – Principal Kelly Newman 
 
Mateo Raymundo Palacios – Grade 3   
Xavier Palacios Ochoa – Grade Kindergarten       
 
Manchester School of Technology – Principal Nancy Donahue 
 
  Lisbeth Santos Lahoz – Grade 12   
Samiyyah DeFrancesco – Grade 9   
Jyzelle Waddell – Grade 9  
 
Antonio Palacios was also welcomed to join his siblings in leading us in the Pledge of Allegiance. 
 
3. A moment of silence was observed.  
 
4. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
Present:  Committee Members Turner, Parr, Want, Taylor, Bergeron, Stewart, 
O’Connell, Potter, St. John, Garrity, Hamer, O’Neil-Wong, Smith and 
Mayor Ruais. 
 
Absent: Committee Members Georges and Bergeron.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 2 of 27 
 
 
 
5.       RECOGNITIONS 
 
Vice Chair O'Connell recognized Committee Member Chris Potter, Ward 7, who was attending his 
final meeting as a member of the Board of School Committee.  He explained that the Board typically 
holds a formal recognition for departing members and presents a token of appreciation; however, as 
it had only recently become known that this would be Committee Member Potter's final meeting, the 
formal presentation would be scheduled for a later date when he would be available to return. 
 
Vice Chair O'Connell nevertheless took the opportunity to publicly thank Committee Member Potter 
for his five years of service to the Board, Ward 7, and the City of Manchester. He spoke about the 
considerable amount of work Committee Member Potter completed outside of public meetings and 
specifically recognized his attention to detail, preparation, due diligence, and willingness to identify 
areas in which policies or proposals could be improved.  He also acknowledged Committee Member 
Potter's work on important Board matters, including implementation of the minimum wage, and 
thanked him for the time and service he had given to Manchester's students, educators, families, and 
residents. 
 
Committee Member Potter thanked the Board for the recognition. 
 
PUBLIC FORUM 
 
6. The purpose of the public forum is to give the residents of Manchester the opportunity to 
address the board.  All people wishing to speak will have up to three (3) minutes to do so, 
and any comments must be directed to the chair.  Any resident wishing to speak will come 
forward to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when recognized and 
give their comments.  
 
Speakers may offer comments on school operations and programs that concern them.  In 
public session, however, the Board shall not hear personal complaints of school personnel or 
complaints against any person connected with the District.  Other channels are provided for 
Board consideration and disposition of legitimate complaints involving  school district
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 3 of 27 
 
employees, which should be referred to Dr. Chmiel.  Speakers are requested to refrain from 
providing confidential information during this comment period.  Any comments that are 
given regarding personnel matters, will not be responded to by the Board or Administration 
during the public meeting, as these items should be discussed in non-public session.   
 
There was no one present wishing to give public comment. 
 
a. If there is no one else present wishing to speak, a motion is in order to take all 
comments under advisement and further to receive and file any written 
documentation presented and to table the remaining minutes for public comment to 
the end of the meeting for those that have not already spoken. 
 
 
7. Response to Public Comment 
 
As no comments were given, there were no responses. 
 
 
 
8.   PRESENTATIONS 
 
a. Multi-Tiered Systems of Support for Behavioral Health Overview and  Update – by Stacy 
Champey, Executive Director of Safe and Supportive Schools 
 
Stacy Champey, Executive Director of Safe and Supportive Schools, provided the Board with 
an overview and progress update regarding the District's Multi-Tiered System of Support for 
Behavioral Health, or MTSS-B.  She explained that MTSS-B is part of the District's broader 
Safe and Supportive Schools work and is designed as a comprehensive system rather than an 
individual program or short-term initiative. The framework incorporates behavioral health, 
mental health, positive school climate, intervention, violence prevention, data, professional 
development, and community partnerships.  She emphasized that meaningful systems change 
takes time. Research indicates that initiatives can require two to four years to reach full 
implementation and that measurable student outcomes may take additional time to emerge. 
She noted that the District has intentionally remained committed to this work over a number 
of years rather than repeatedly abandoning initiatives and replacing them with new programs.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 4 of 27 
 
Ms. Champey reviewed the history of the work, noting that it began prior to the current 
strategic plan.  A pilot was launched at Wilson School in 2018 to establish schoolwide 
positive behavior supports. Beginning in 2020, the District expanded systems work to more 
closely integrate community mental health services into schools. 
 
Over the subsequent years, the District developed teams in schools focused on: 
 Positive school climate; 
 Behavioral intervention; 
 Mental health supports; 
 Schoolwide prevention; 
 Violence prevention; 
 Behavioral threat assessment and management; and 
 Coordinated student support. 
 
Ms. Champey reported that the District had secured more than $10 million in state and 
federal grant funding to assist in developing this work and had collaborated with national 
researchers and technical assistance centers.  The framework was developed using both 
District and community data. Identified areas of need included student behavior, mental 
health, school safety, suspension rates, and access to behavioral health interventions.  An 
important objective of the work is to reduce exclusionary discipline, including out-of-school 
suspensions, while ensuring schools remain safe and students receive appropriate behavioral 
and mental health interventions. 
 
Ms. Champey reported that community mental health clinicians are currently integrated into 
14 District schools through a model designed to remain sustainable beyond the life of 
individual grants. Seven additional schools were reported as having access to services 
through the Mental Health Center of Greater Manchester, with additional expansion 
anticipated through collaboration with community partners. 
 
The District is also: 
 Piloting restorative practices at Weston Elementary School;
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 5 of 27 
 
 Developing a Student Success model in the high schools for students experiencing 
repeated suspensions or at risk of disengaging from school; 
 Expanding trauma-responsive strategies at the elementary level; 
 Developing an early-warning indicator dashboard to help school teams identify 
students needing support before concerns become chronic or escalate; 
 Maintaining behavioral threat assessment and management teams in every school; 
 Utilizing a school safety concern reporting process monitored at both the District and 
law enforcement levels; 
 Coordinating professional development and coaching across schools; and 
 Developing a long-term sustainability and funding strategy. 
 
Ms. Champey stressed that the District is attempting to align these efforts rather than operate 
multiple unrelated systems. Positive school climate, mental health, violence prevention, staff 
well-being, community partnerships, and student behavioral supports are being organized 
under the broader Safe and Supportive Schools structure. 
 
Ms. Champey explained that the MTSS-B framework is rooted in prevention.  Every school 
now has identified schoolwide behavior expectations, a method for teaching those 
expectations, a positive acknowledgement system, and a pathway through which students can 
be referred for additional support when necessary.  She reviewed social-emotional learning 
programming across the District. Second Step is used primarily in elementary schools and is 
being expanded to preschool. Wayfinder is being introduced at the four middle schools. 
Beech Street Elementary School continues to use Toolbox, while Gosler Park Elementary 
School continues to use Leader in Me. Ms. Champey explained that those schools had 
longstanding programs aligned with appropriate standards and were implementing them 
effectively, so the District did not believe it was necessary to replace successful 
programming solely for the purpose of making every building identical. 
 
At the middle and high school levels, the District has also developed the Reach Out, Speak 
Up campaign. The campaign is intended to encourage students to reach out when they need 
mental health support and to speak up when they have concerns regarding school safety or
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 6 of 27 
 
another person's safety.  The District has been developing posters that identify actual staff 
members and School Resource Officers so students are able to connect a name and face with 
the adults available to assist them. 
 
Ms. Champey explained that student needs often extend across several areas at once, 
including behavior, social-emotional development, mental health, housing, and family 
circumstances.  Historically, multiple teams might have addressed separate pieces of a 
student's needs. Under the developing model, schools are working toward a single behavioral 
health intervention team that can review concerns collectively and develop a more 
coordinated support plan.  She cautioned that the teams are at different stages of 
implementation. Some are relatively new, while others have been operating for two or more 
years. 
 
Central High School was identified as an example of a school that has moved from more 
isolated systems toward a coordinated team structure involving school staff, two mental 
health agencies, and a Student Success position. 
 
Ms. Champey emphasized the role of coaching in moving the work from planning to actual 
implementation. Coaches assist school teams in understanding expectations, determining 
next steps, maintaining progress, and using data for action planning.  The District has grown 
from one schoolwide team in 2018 to approximately 20 schoolwide teams and 20 
intervention teams.  Implementation is measured both at the school and District levels. 
Annual assessments help determine whether schools are putting required components into 
place with fidelity. 
 
The District is also monitoring outcomes, including: 
 Office discipline referrals; 
 Suspensions; 
 School climate; 
 Access to behavioral and mental health supports; and 
 Student engagement.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 7 of 27 
 
 
Ms. Champey reported that the staff climate survey response rate had increased from 
approximately 29 percent to 62 percent over two years. Districtwide areas needing additional 
attention included student behavior and parent involvement. 
 
The family survey response rate more than doubled to approximately 7.2 percent, 
representing approximately 815 families. While overall family scores were above the 
District's identified target, Ms. Champey acknowledged that participation remained much 
lower than desired. 
 
Board Members questions and comments included: 
1. Committee Member Stewart expressed concern regarding the family survey response 
rate and asked what barriers may be preventing broader participation.  Ms. Champey 
explained that some existing survey questions may not apply equally well to all 
families. For example, questions regarding parent-teacher conferences may not reflect 
the experience of families at all grade levels, and questions regarding volunteering 
may produce lower scores simply because working parents are unable to volunteer 
during the school day.  She stated that the District would continue reviewing the 
survey instrument and its communication strategy and would work toward again 
increasing the response rate. 
2. The timing of the survey was also discussed. A Committee Member noted that 
families often receive numerous surveys during the spring and suggested that survey 
fatigue may affect participation. Ms. Champey stated that the District had 
administered the survey at various times between March and May and was open to 
considering a different time of year. 
3. Committee members also asked how the District obtains feedback directly from 
students.  Ms. Champey explained that a student climate survey exists, but 
administering such a survey Districtwide would require parent consent and significant 
staff time. As an alternative, the District has been using student focus groups.  She 
noted that the Reach Out, Speak Up posters identifying specific adults within schools 
came directly from student feedback. Students had indicated that, although they may
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 8 of 27 
 
be told at the beginning of the year who can help them, they do not always know who 
those individuals are or what their roles are. 
4. The Board discussed how the District determined which social-emotional learning 
programs would be used.  Ms. Champey explained that Second Step was selected 
because it is evidence-based and aligned with applicable standards. As additional 
schools became interested in the program, the District was able to scale 
implementation. 
5. Committee members asked whether Second Step includes a family engagement 
component. Ms. Champey confirmed that it does and explained that, as schools 
become more experienced with the core curriculum, the District can deepen 
implementation by adding family components and other features. 
6. Committee members noted the value of parents understanding and using the same 
language and strategies students are learning at school. 
7. The Board asked about the long-term sustainability of the work as Project AWARE 
grant funding approaches its conclusion.  Ms. Champey stated that sustainability had 
been considered from the beginning. The District is working with Dr. Chmiel, 
Assistant Superintendents, the City's grant writer, law enforcement, and community 
partners to identify which positions or programs can transition from one funding 
source to another.  She described "braided funding" as strategically combining 
multiple grant and partner resources to support a common system. One grant may 
initially fund a position or program while another future grant or community partner 
may assume responsibility for a portion of that work. 
8. Ms. Champey used violence prevention and the Student Success model as examples 
of programs that may begin under Project AWARE and later transition to other 
Department of Justice, juvenile justice, District, or community-partner funding 
sources.  She acknowledged that the process is complex and requires ongoing 
coordination, particularly when funding requirements change. 
9. Board members thanked Ms. Champey for the presentation and praised both the work 
itself and the way the information demonstrated progress over time, including clear 
historical comparisons and measurable implementation data.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 9 of 27 
 
9. ACTION AGENDA 
 
There were no items on the action agenda this evening. 
 
 
10. CONSENT AGENDA (ITEMS 10 – 17)  
 
a. Mayor Ruais advises if you desire to remove any of the following items from the Consent 
Agenda, please so indicate.  If none of the items are to be removed, only one motion will 
be taken at the conclusion of the presentation.  
 
 
No items were removed from the Consent agenda for discussion. 
 
The approved consent agenda was as follows: 
 
b. Approval of minutes from the Board of School Committee meetings on: August 31 st, 
2026 Special meeting and the September 14, 2026. 
 
c. Report(s) of the Committee on Policy, if available.      
 
1. Students 520: Discipline and Due Process policy proposed revisions   
2. Student Code of Conduct Proposed Revisions        
    
d. Report(s) of the Committee of Teaching and Learning, if available.     
 
1. Policy - Instruction 743: Remote and Virtual Learning       
2. New Policy - Instruction 767: Career Exploration, Readiness, Pathways and 
Credentialing 
3. Policy Instruction 703: Curriculum Development and Instruction   
4. Policy Instruction 729: Middle and High School Grading      
 
e. Report(s) of the Committee of Finance and Facilities, if available.  
  
f. Report(s) of the Committee of Student Conduct, if available.  
 
g. Report(s) of the Committee on Education Legislation, if available.  
 
h. Report(s) of the Joint School Buildings Committee (City Committee).
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 10 of 27 
 
i. Special Committees, if applicable: 
 
o Report from the Special Committee on Athletics, if available. 
 
On motion of Committee Member O’Connell, duly seconded by Committee  Member Turner, it was 
moved to approve the balance of the consent agenda.  All were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
COMMUNICATIONS 
 
11. Superintendent’s Communications.  
 
a) Superintendent Updates (Please see attached memo) 
 
Dr. Chmiel advised the Board that a written memorandum had been provided and would be attached 
to the meeting materials online. Administration provided updates regarding enrollment, in-District 
transfers, class sizes, state assessments, personnel, transportation, operations, athletics, and upcoming 
events. 
 
The Administration discussed the following items: 
1. Enrollment 
 Dr. Chmiel stated that the total enrollment was reported at 11,732 students, including 
preschool and out-of-District Manchester School of Technology CTE students. 
 When preschool and out-of-District MST CTE students were removed, K-12 enrollment 
was reported at 11,065 students. 
 Dr. Chmiel noted that the District ended the previous school year with 11,053 K-12 
students. Current enrollment was therefore approximately 12 students above the June 
2026 level, demonstrating that overall District enrollment remained relatively consistent 
with the prior year. 
 The Administration will continue monitoring enrollment, particularly shifts occurring 
among individual schools and grade levels.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 11 of 27 
 
2. In-District Transfers 
 
Dr. Chmiel reported that approximately 221 in-District transfer requests had been received and 148 
had been approved.  Now that the school year was underway and students had begun settling into 
their classrooms, the District had paused new in-District transfer requests. Requests will reopen in 
May for families seeking transfers for the following school year.  The Administration intends to 
conduct an internal review of the transfer process. 
 
Board Members questions and comments included: 
1. Committee Member Potter asked whether approved transfer requests had resulted in 
additional involuntary transfers when neighborhood schools reached capacity and how 
transportation was being handled. Dr. Chmiel explained that the District attempts, whenever 
possible, to maintain approximately two open seats at each school for children living within 
the attendance area. Several schools, however, were already at or near capacity and could not 
maintain those spaces. 
2. For parent-requested transfers, families are responsible for transportation. When the District 
involuntarily transfers a student because the home school does not have available capacity, 
the District provides transportation. 
3. The Administration indicated that it had not observed a significant increase in transportation 
needs attributable to involuntary transfers. 
4. Committee Member Hamer requested that, once enrollment had stabilized, the Board receive 
a school-by-school breakdown showing the number of students not attending their 
neighborhood school as well as the schools receiving students from outside their attendance 
areas.  The Administration agreed that the information could be provided. 
 
3. Class Sizes – Elementary Schools 
 
Ms. Doherty reminded the Board that District policy establishes a maximum class size of 20 students 
in Grades K-4.  The majority of elementary classrooms remained at or below that level; however, 
several schools and grade levels continued to exceed the policy.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 12 of 27 
 
Schools identified for continued monitoring included: 
 Gosler Park; 
 Green Acres; 
 Highland; 
 Jewett; 
 Smith; and 
 Weston. 
 
Most classes exceeding the maximum contained 21 or 22 students, with a smaller number reaching 
23.  Green Acres remained a particular area of concern, especially in Grades 2 through 4, where all 
classrooms were reported above the class-size policy.  Beech Street had shown positive movement 
and was reported at or below 20 students in all elementary classrooms. It was stated that enrollment 
and class sizes would continue to be monitored and adjustments made where reasonably possible. 
 
4. Class Sizes – Middle Schools 
 
Mr. Roth reported the middle school enrollment at approximately 3,277 students across Grades 5 
through 8.  The District policy establishes a maximum class size of 25 at this level.  The middle 
school class sizes were explained as: 
1. Hillside Middle School was reported at approximately 966 students, with two classes 
exceeding 25. 
2. McLaughlin Middle School was reported at approximately 819 students and had 29 
classes above 25. Most were at 26 or 27 students, with a smaller number ranging from 
28 to 30. A significant portion of the larger classes were in unified arts, including 
music and art. 
3. Parkside Middle School was reported at approximately 746 students, with three 
classes exceeding 25. 
4. Southside Middle School was also reported at approximately 746 students, with 12 
classes above 25, all within Grade 8. Courses identified included ELA, social studies, 
mathematics, science, and physical education.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 13 of 27 
 
Mr. Roth indicated that the majority of middle school classes remained at or below policy and that 
opportunities to rebalance or adjust sections would continue to be explored. 
 
Board questions and comments included: 
1. Concerns were raised about Grade 8 science classes at Southside containing 26 or 27 
students when District policy identifies a lower maximum for laboratory classes. 
2. It was asked whether larger classes could prevent students from participating in 
hands-on laboratory work. Dr. Chmiel explained that the District did not currently 
have budget capacity simply to add additional teaching positions. When an additional 
kindergarten classroom was recently added at Green Acres, for example, the District 
had to reallocate an existing vacancy to fund the position. 
3. The Administration agreed to review the Southside science sections for possible 
rebalancing. 
4. Dr. Chmiel also noted that middle school laboratory activities have changed 
significantly over time. Many current activities use household or lower-risk materials 
rather than the types of chemicals historically associated with science laboratories. 
Nevertheless, administration would make efforts to bring classes closer to established 
maximums. 
5. The possibility of assigning teachers a sixth class was also discussed. Administration 
stated that this strategy is already used in some circumstances. However, adding a 
section can significantly affect schedules throughout a middle school and is most 
appropriate where enrollment substantially exceeds available capacity rather than 
when a class is only one student over the maximum. 
6. The Board also asked whether teachers holding dual certifications could be deployed 
differently to assist with class-size issues. Administration responded that certification 
is considered when staffing schools but that middle school schedules are 
interconnected and changes to one teacher's schedule often affect several others. 
7. Dr. Chmiel reiterated that she did not recommend increasing the class-size limits 
contained in District policy and agreed that smaller classes remain preferable for both 
students and staff.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 14 of 27 
 
 
5. Class Sizes – High Schools 
 
Dr. Espinola reported that: 
 West High School had 18 classes with 25 or more students, although none exceeded 30; 
 Central High School had four classes with more than 25 students; 
 Memorial High School had 13 classes exceeding 25 and 10 special education classes 
exceeding 12 students; and 
 MST continued to be monitored closely, with 26 instructional or support classes above the 
listed maximum. 
She explained that high school scheduling is particularly complex because moving a student from 
one section can affect English, math, science, electives, lunch periods, and graduation requirements. 
 
The District will continue monitoring sections and making adjustments when feasible. 
 
6. 2026 State Assessment Results 
 
Ms. Doherty  provided the Board with a one-page summary of the 2026 state assessment results 
following a more detailed review by the Teaching and Learning Committee.  The results showed 
improvement across all three assessed areas. 
 
During discussion, Committee Member Potter highlighted gains of approximately: 
 3 percentage points in reading/writing; 
 2 percentage points in mathematics; and 
 3 percentage points in science. 
 
He also highlighted larger improvements in certain grade levels, including an approximately eight-
point increase in Grade 5 reading/writing.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 15 of 27 
 
Committee Member Potter stated that academic proficiency is a lagging indicator and encouraged 
the Board to recognize the connection between current student outcomes and investments made over 
previous years in professional development, staffing, and class-size reduction. 
 
Dr. Chmiel encouraged Board members and the public to review the full Teaching and Learning 
presentation, noting that the one-page summary was intended to provide Board members with 
accessible information they could share with constituents.  It was emphasized that, although 
additional work remains, the data reflects encouraging progress and that the District's next step is to 
identify successful practices and continue strengthening them. 
 
7. Hopeville: How to Win the Reading Wars 
 
Ms. Doherty announced that Manchester School District educators, families, and community 
members were invited to a screening of Hopeville: How to Win the Reading Wars on October 8 from 
4:00 to 7:00 p.m., followed by a panel discussion.  The event was being held in partnership with 
UNH and the International Dyslexia Association and was intended to provide information about 
evidence-based reading instruction.  Teachers would also have an opportunity to participate in a 
screening and panel discussion during the October 9 District professional development day. 
 
8. Personnel Update 
 
Michelle Evans reported that the personnel report included several key hires, including a Naval 
Science position at West High School and the final vacant DLI Spanish teaching position for the 
Bakersville DLI program.  The District had reduced 41 positions through attrition at the end of June 
2026 as part of the budget process. Administration stated that resignations and retirements occurring 
beyond those 41 reductions were being replaced.  From May through September 28, 2026, the 
District had made 182 replacement hires, consisting of: 
 93 teachers; 
 32 paraprofessionals; and 
 57 various support positions.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 16 of 27 
 
At the time of the meeting, the District had: 
 20 open teaching positions, including 11 special education teaching positions; and 
 13 open paraprofessional positions. 
 
HR continues to work with building administrators on targeted recruitment efforts, including social 
media campaigns, college career fairs, and other outreach.  The District representatives attended the 
UNH Fall Career Fair in Durham on September 16.  Ms. Evans also indicated that employee 
retention data would be analyzed once state reporting information became available, which was 
anticipated in mid-to-late October. 
 
9. Home-to-School Transportation 
 
Dr. Espinola reported continuing challenges with home-to-school transportation, which included: 
1. Eight vehicles were out of service at the time of the meeting: 
 Two awaiting parts; 
 Two in the shop; 
 Two with repairs underway; and 
 Two awaiting repairs. 
2. Bridge construction and repair work had also required several routes to be adjusted 
and had contributed to delays. 
3. Hillside Bus 1 did not have a permanently assigned driver and had experienced 
repeated delays. Administration was attempting to rotate coverage and identify 
temporary solutions so the same group of students would not be consistently affected. 
4. The District continued actively recruiting bus drivers. Administration noted that each 
additional driver improves the District's ability to cover routes consistently and 
reduces the daily need to reassign personnel. 
 
Board members questions and comments included: 
1. It was noted that Hillside Bus 1 had been approximately 45 minutes late each day during the 
prior week because there was no assigned driver.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 17 of 27 
 
2. Concern was expressed that students whose families cannot provide alternate transportation 
could lose approximately 45 minutes of instruction every day, which is inconsistent with the 
District's emphasis on student attendance. 
3. The Board thanked administration for working to find temporary solutions and encouraged 
the District to continue exploring additional recruitment strategies, including whether signing 
bonuses, stipends, or other incentives might be possible within budget constraints. 
4. The Administration was also asked to consider adding bus driver vacancies to the job 
openings information routinely presented to the Board. 
5. Vice Chair O'Connell asked how many buses the District currently owns and how many are 
actually being operated.  The Administration estimated that the District had approximately 56 
buses, but only approximately 30 drivers were available for combined morning and afternoon 
operations. 
6. Vice Chair O'Connell asked whether that effectively meant a substantial portion of the fleet 
was sitting unused because drivers were unavailable. Administration confirmed that buses 
were available and additional vehicles could be put into service if additional drivers were 
hired. 
7. The Board requested historical data regarding the typical number of buses out of service 
under prior transportation operations. 
8. Vice Chair O'Connell also suggested that the District review the appropriate long-term fleet 
size and replacement cycle. Historically, a fleet of approximately 50 to 56 buses combined 
with the purchase of approximately five buses annually had produced roughly a ten-year 
replacement cycle. He questioned whether that remained the appropriate model given the 
District's current operating needs.  Administration agreed to review the information. 
 
10. Specialized Transportation 
 
Mr. Roth reported that approximately 842 students were actively receiving specialized 
transportation.  The specialized transportation team was coordinating approximately: 
 89 buses and vans; 
 89 drivers; and 
 40 monitors.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 18 of 27 
 
The team continues to address changes in student services, addresses, schools, schedules, and pick-
up and drop-off locations.  He stated that the number of immediate transportation concerns and 
telephone calls was beginning to decrease as routes stabilized and outstanding information was 
resolved. 
 
11. Student Behavior on Buses 
 
The Administration reported that student behavior had contributed to the loss of additional bus 
drivers.  The District is working with building administrators to reinforce expectations that school 
buses must be safe and respectful environments for both students and drivers.  It was emphasized 
that driver recruitment alone will not resolve the problem if the District is unable to retain existing 
drivers. 
 
Questions and comments from the Board included: 
1. Board members discussed the significant responsibility placed upon a driver who must safely 
operate a large vehicle while supervising a bus full of students. 
2. The Administration explained that bus behavior has been a concern in prior years as well and 
that principals or assistant principals have, when necessary, ridden buses to assist with 
behavior and restore order. 
3. Dr. Espinola explained that the issue currently appears particularly significant at the middle 
school level. 
4. The Administration is exploring ways to build stronger relationships between students and 
drivers. Ideas include inviting drivers to attend middle school lunches and participate in 
school spirit weeks.  The goal is for students to see the driver not simply as an unfamiliar 
adult operating the bus but as a member of the school community with whom they have an 
ongoing relationship. 
5. The Administration stated that relationships can influence behavior and that these efforts may 
improve the climate on buses over time. 
6. Committee Member Stewart asked whether families could become more directly involved in 
responding to student misconduct on buses.  The Administration confirmed that parents are 
contacted when their child is involved in behavioral incidents.
September 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 19 of 27 
 
7. The possibility of parent volunteers riding buses was briefly discussed. Administration stated 
that any such proposal would require volunteers to complete the appropriate screening 
process and would also raise student privacy considerations. 
8. Dr. Chmiel emphasized that students can lose transportation privileges for misconduct. 
Progressive discipline is used on buses just as it is in schools, and families were reminded 
that transportation is a privilege that students are expected to use responsibly. 
9. Committee Member St. John raised a constituent concern regarding bus stops on Hughes 
Road where students reportedly had to cross the roadway.  He expressed concern that the 
road was unsafe for children to cross. 
10. The Administration indicated that it believed the issue had been corrected and encouraged 
families with continuing transportation safety concerns to contact the District directly so 
concerns could be addressed promptly. 
 
12. Operations – Pest Concerns 
 
Dr. Espinola reported an increase in pest concerns across District buildings as the seasons changed. 
Reported concerns included mice, cockroaches, and ants.  Cockroach activity had been reported at

 Monitor whether services remain appropriate; and 
 Provide sufficient staffing for students requiring specialized instruction. 
 
The Administration explained that the IEP process includes multiple levels of review. Case 
managers facilitate student IEPs, building-level LEAs review them for procedural compliance and 
timelines, and District special education leadership also reviews plans before they are finalized and 
returned to families.  When a certified teacher vacancy exists in a self-contained or specialized 
classroom, administration works with building leadership to develop manageable staffing rotations 
and bring other certified staff into the classroom to ensure students continue receiving required 
instruction and services. 
 
3. Committee Member Potter asked specifically whether vacancies were creating additional 
strain despite those systems.  The Administration acknowledged that the volume of work is 
significant and that staff are being deployed to schools and classrooms to provide additional 
support where needed. 
4. Vice Chair O'Connell stated that his concern extended beyond technical compliance with IEP 
requirements.  He questioned what happens operationally when a teacher is absent from a 
specialized or self-contained program and there is no equivalent teacher readily available 
within the building.  His concern was that existing special education teachers could be 
serving larger groups of students or carrying additional responsibilities because of vacancies.  
The Administration acknowledged that the vacancies create compression on existing staff. 
5. Dr. Chmiel stated that special education teacher shortages are a national, state, and local 
workforce issue and not unique to Manchester.  She acknowledged that staff workloads 
increase when qualified candidates cannot be found and that this is not the preferred situation 
for students or employees.  In response, the District has used strategies including: 
 Paying some staff to teach an additional sixth period; 
 Rotating certified staff into classrooms requiring coverage; 
 Working directly with building LEAs and principals; 
 Reviewing student schedules to improve deployment of available staff; 
 Recruiting through local colleges and universities; 
 Working with the State on certification pathways; and

 Moving qualified candidates to schools as quickly as possible when applications are 
received. 
 
Dr. Chmiel thanked special education teachers and staff for their efforts to maintain services despite 
staffing shortages.  She stated that the District would hire qualified candidates immediately if 
enough applicants were available and noted that the number of vacancies had been higher in 
previous years. 
 
The Administration also explained that District staff work directly with principals and LEAs when a 
building identifies a staffing or scheduling issue.  In one instance, additional District support was 
brought into a school to review schedules and recommend changes so required services could be 
deployed more effectively. 
 
Dr. Chmiel emphasized that ensuring student coverage is a shared responsibility involving District 
leadership, principals, LEAs, and teachers and thanked staff across the system for continuing to meet 
those responsibilities.
